In this work, we establish that a generalised rotational surface of the type described by Chen and Murata is flat if the surface's pointwise Gauss map follows a specific exponential decay pattern.

A key challenge in computer vision is developing robust models that generalize well to different environments.  Deep learning has led to significant advancements in visual tasks, but models trained for specific datasets often fail to perform optimally in new settings.  To address this issue, researchers have developed methods to pretrain models using unsupervised or weakly supervised learning techniques.  This study proposes a new approach to pretraining deep networks by leveraging scene geometry rather than object categories.  By training on openly accessible internet images, the method aims to demonstrate the value of global data for model generalization.  To achieve this, a new dataset of 2 million images is introduced, along with a novel architecture that efficiently encodes scene geometry from various perspectives.  A self-supervised learning method is developed to exploit scene geometry for unsupervised image annotation, enabling the model to be evaluated on benchmark datasets without needing labeled data.  Results show that the proposed scene-geometry-based pretraining leads to improved performance across a range of scene recognition tasks and demonstrates enhanced generalization capabilities.

Time-series data is ubiquitous in various industries, making the understanding of time-series data crucial. TCube is a comprehensive system designed to facilitate time-series data analysis through visualizations and automated machine learning pipelines, leveraging visual cues to aid in decision-making. TCube's capabilities include the automatic construction of data analysis pipelines, allowing users to leverage their visual intuition. TCube's design prioritizes simplicity and interpretability, enabling users to gain insight into the pipeline and data learning process. TCube's performance is outstanding, rivaling human performance with a relative risk reduction of 13.5% (95% CI: 0.02 to 0.27), particularly excelling in tasks requiring precise results.

We examine the impact of one-loop dimension-6 and dimension-8 operators involving four leptons on the $C_P$-odd $b\to s\mu^+\mu^-$ transition in the context of $B$-meson rare decays on the RHC experiment. Our analysis is carried out within the framework of the effective Hamiltonian, with particular emphasis placed on the $B^0_\tau\to\mu^+\mu^-$ and $B^0_\tau\to\mu^+\mu^- \mu^+\mu^-$ processes. We derive dimension-8 Wilson coefficient constraints by considering interference between dimension-6 and dimension-8 Wilson coefficients in the $B^0_\tau\to\mu^+\mu^-$ process. Furthermore, with upcoming improvements in experimental precision for the branching fraction of $B^0\to\mu^+\mu^-$ and $B^0_\tau\to\mu^+\mu^- \mu^+\mu^-$, we investigate the constraints that can be placed on dimension-8 Wilson coefficients alongside existing dimension-6 constraints.

The Ising model on a Cayley tree based on a free group of two generators is analyzed, with the tree's structure corresponding to the tree's universal covering. Using the momentum method and integrating the influence of the tree's infinite depth, an expression for the free energy of the Ising model is derived.

The geometric structure of phase space offers valuable insights into how certain partial differential equation solutions behave. This is particularly evident in the case of the wave equation on Lorentzian manifolds, where specific types of metrics lead to areas of insufficient solution behavior. In contrast, new results show that, when the metric satisfies certain curvature conditions, solution properties of smoothness and microlocalization remain preserved across a range of different metric options.

This research proposes a novel application of Long Short-Term Memory networks to enhance Japanese word segmentation accuracy. A previously developed system, which combined Hidden Markov Models and Feature-based Undirected Models, served as the foundation. To further improve accuracy, an method involving Long Short-Term Memory was introduced. Japanese characteristics such as morphological complexity and the absence of space characters were taken into consideration. An extensive dataset consisting of 400,000 words from various sources was used to train the model. As a result, significant accuracy gains were observed across multiple evaluation criteria, including linearity, whole accuracy, and the relative improvement in character-based error rates.

Stack Overflow, a widely-used Q&A platform for coders, boasts extensive
external knowledge bases in the form of over 55,000 external links tagged
"reference" by users. Our investigation into these links aims to offer
developers, managers, and researchers valuable insights for effective
knowledge management. Our findings indicate that there is a core group of
popular references, such as documentation sites and code repositories,
consistently shared by users. Interestingly, the size of a Stack Overflow
community positively influences external knowledge contribution. Our
analysis also shows a notable difference between questions and answers
regarding external knowledge usage, with questions tending to reference more
external resources. Furthermore, our data indicates that the type of programming
language being learned impacts external knowledge sharing.

The presence of a flat rotation curve in the outer regions of many galaxies is typically attributed to a constant density core in their halo's rotation curve model. However, simulations of structure formation often produce cuspy halos with non-flat inner rotation curves, leading to a discrepancy. To reconcile this, variations of the standard cold dark matter model have been proposed, aiming to produce isothermal cores. Our research demonstrates that achieving diverse galaxy rotation curves, particularly with isothermal cores, requires fluctuations in the fluctuations of the gravitational potential spectrum, which peaks at a specific scale corresponding to the galaxies' bulge. Notably, our findings show that these isothermal core configurations are consistent with minimum isocurvature fluctuations, provided that the fluctuations in their halo match those of their bulge, leading to a potential parameter space for isocurvature models that was previously excluded.

To inspire action from others in addressing climate change, it is essential to comprehend how to effectively convey urgent information to a broader audience. One approach to do this involves leveraging social networks to disseminate climate change information, but simply disseminating messages may not be sufficient to motivate individuals to take action. Understanding their personal values may help tailor the urgency of the information shared, but this requires an accurate prediction of their values based on available information. We developed an algorithm that utilizes the Twitter dataset to forecast individual values by analyzing their connections and interactions. Our model compares its predictions to a baseline and shows and surpasss the results in an online simulation, demonstrating its ability to identify and classify values from the Twitter user network.

In this research, our primary objective is to enhance the accuracy of extracting clinical symptoms from diverse medical datasets, particularly those from non-English sources.  For this objective, we've developed a comprehensive English-German clinical symptom extraction framework that utilizes a pre-trained model and an enhanced attention-based method pre-fine-tuned on an extensive medical dataset, ClinicalBERT.  This pre-trained model can be easily adapted for specific tasks by fine-tuning it on relevant datasets while maintaining consistent results across various clinical domains.  For example, our model was initially trained on a cardiology dataset and successfully transferred to two additional datasets in the same field, as well as a second field of urology, demonstrating consistent performance and high accuracy in symptom extraction and patient signal classification.  Notably, our approach achieved superior results compared to classical techniques and other state-of-the-art models, particularly in the challenging task of transferring learned abilities to unfamiliar clinical domains.

Autonomous vehicles rely on partial observations to make driving decisions, which has led to the development of Reinforcement Learning techniques for handling this challenge. Neural networks have been used to process and extract relevant information from these inputs, which can result in overfitting when combined with Reinforcement Learning due to the increased risk of bias and noise propagation. To address this limitation, Variational Auto-Encoders are used to compress input information and reduce overfitting in our proposed FROST algorithm. By integrating VAEs with a policy network and using LSTMs to model temporal dependencies, the algorithm achieves better performance and a new state-of-the-art result on the CARLA autonomous driving platform. Specifically, the application of FROST in a partially observable lane-keeping task demonstrates improved results when compared to other methods. Furthermore, the model's generalization capabilities are evaluated and demonstrated to excel in both homogeneous and heterogeneous settings.

We propose TANN, a novel quantized neural network, as a universal classifier capable of rivaling traditional ANNs in accuracy while significantly (up to 99.5%) reducing power consumption with minimal performance loss of under 0.5%. TANN's innovative design leverages time-domain activation values, a vector error mapping technique, and adaptive quantization levels to minimize quantization errors. Furthermore, TANN can be effectively pruned by utilizing the Vector Mean Error metric, enabling the removal of redundant nodes and layers in a neural network. The effectiveness of TANN is substantiated by its superior performance on multiple image classification datasets, including CIFAR-100 and ImageNet.

In high magnetic fields, the structural characteristics of spin-polarized strange quark matter are investigated through thermodynamic analysis.  Both the phase transition between quark matter and hadronic matter and the equation of state (EOS) are significantly influenced by the transition, and this information is crucial for understanding the interior of neutron stars.  Our research indicates that in high magnetic fields, neutron star radii can be either larger or smaller than those predicted without a magnetic field, and this radius can even be used to constrain this field.

Pando is a multi-device personal computing system, similar to Cloud computing, that leverages multiple personal devices to enhance computational capabilities. It distributes tasks across multiple devices, such as smartphones and laptops, to improve computational throughput and data ownership. In a study, the researchers evaluated Pando's performance by comparing its computational throughput to that of a single device and found it significantly (up to 2.7 times) more efficient. They also demonstrated that Pando offers comparable reliability to a single device and slightly lower data transfer costs compared to Cloud computing (up to 99.67% lower).

This research introduces an innovative adaptive sampling technique to improve nystrom method efficiency for estimating eigenvalues and singular values. By strategically selecting samples, the approach enhances nystrom method accuracy while using the same resources. Furthermore, the enhanced method allows for faster convergence and a more precise outcome using fewer samples.

We provide a detailed analysis of the structure of sets containing points with
specific properties related to $\beta$-expansions in non-integer bases. Our study
focuses on subsets formed by the intersection of intervals with significant properties.
As a result, we can now visualize these sets in two dimensions and better
understand their measure and topological characteristics. Our findings also
include an exploration of points with specific properties related to approximations
by fractions in two dimensions, as well as the development of a lower bound
for the measure of sets containing points with specific properties related to
unique expansions in non-integer bases.

We study SO(N_c) gauge theories with N_F quark flavors and SU(N_c) gauge invariance.
The theories lack a determinant term in the quark sector due to the presence of a gauge invariant bilinear, leading to an SU(N_F) chiral symmetry.
Due to this symmetry, the theory sector sector exhibits degenerate states, preventing a direct mass acquisition by the Wilson fermions without breaking the symmetry.
To overcome this issue, we introduce a linear term in the fermion sector without compromising the symmetry, thereby enabling a direct quark mass acquisition.
However, this introduction results in a non-local effective action.
To resolve this problem, we propose a path integral formulation for the theories with Wilson fermions without a determinant term.
The formulation involves an auxiliary spin system and an integration over a non-compact imaginary gauge field.
The theories under consideration encompass a wide range of SO(N_c) gauge theories with Wilson fermions.
The formulation is then applied to SO(3) and USp(2) gauge theories with Wilson fermions and non-compact imaginary gauge fields.

Explainability methods aid in gaining insights into complex models, but their application often lacks clarity due to ambiguous results and partial understanding of machine learning processes. To address these issues, we propose a new framework called Disentangled Attribution Curves (DAC), which enhances visualization and analysis of machine learning models. Our framework's core innovation lies in its ability to introduce order among model inputs, allowing for more comprehensive factor analysis. Through use-case demonstrations across machine learning, we demonstrate the benefits of the DAC framework in identifying complex interactions, such as those found in a bike-sharing dataset, and explainable AI dependencies, like those found in a human rights dataset. Ultimately, we hope the DAC framework will empower researchers to gain deeper understanding of their models and promote more transparent AI practices.

Several methods have been developed to protect the privacy of data in federated learning systems. Despite their efforts, most existing approaches in this field have significant limitations, such as high communication costs, incompatibility with various attack types, or only providing partial privacy assurance. In order to address these issues, a new framework called FedDP-SGA is proposed to ensure the privacy of local data for multiple clients in federated learning systems. By combining differential privacy and adversarial training, FedDP-SGA offers a comprehensive solution for various types of attacks and achieves high accuracy while maintaining the privacy of data for multiple clients. Experimental results demonstrate that the framework outperforms other methods in terms of both accuracy and privacy assurance.

Testing drivers is a critical part of the development process for embedded systems, but it's particularly challenging when working with microcontrollers. The limited resources of these devices make it difficult to test their drivers, a problem that our solution aims to address. We have designed a testing framework consisting of two key components: an instruction set that allows drivers to initiate and conclude testing, as well as a hardware abstraction layer for simulating peripheral devices. This framework has been implemented on the TI MSP430 microcontroller and, along with the support of an oscilloscope, enables comprehensive testing even without a connected device.

Conyers et al.'s Calligraffe is a tool that automatically identifies and removes unnecessary system calls in a given application, a task previously only achievable for applications written in a specific programming language, but now possible for those written in Python and PHP through a new, work-stealing based approach called Timeloops, which analyzes the application in multiple threads to significantly reduce processing time, resulting in a substantial speedup, including a notable improvement in complex applications, including Firefox and Chrome.

Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) generates high-dimensional data that poses challenges for effective gene selection and dimensionality reduction. Our work introduces and assesses various methods for selecting dimensions and genes in Euclidean spaces as well as in low-dimensional product spaces. We compare the efficacy of these methods through simulations and real-world experiments, and suggest improvements for existing techniques. Furthermore, we demonstrate that reducing the dimensionality of data in low-dimensional product spaces yields better performance for classification and neighbor-based tasks, outperforming Euclidean spaces by a significant margin of up to 20%. We also developed and tested multiple methods for gene selection, and in collaboration with biologists, interpreted the results to understand the biological context. Our findings indicate that effective Gale-Berlekamp strategies for encoding data can achieve performance comparable to traditional space reductions but require less time and produce more accurate outcomes.

Our research focuses on how various initial conditions and a supermassive black hole's growing mass influence the movement of close stellar orbits in the Galactic Center. We specifically examined various star mass distributions, their impact on energy exchanges between typical and heavy stars, and observed variations in these exchanges across different mass hierarchies. We found that our estimates for energy gain intervals match theoretical predictions from previous studies. Additionally, we analyzed and compared our results with those obtained using a model that assumes uniform mass distribution, and discovered significant differences in these models' predictions for several key parameters.

This research paper explores the application of stochastic Model Predictive Control to address system dynamics influenced by randomness, with a particular focus on high-performance systems such as helicopters and self-driving cars. Due to infrequent occurrences of disturbances in these systems, conventional approaches based on Markov processes are impractical to implement. Consequently, this study formulates a new framework for stochastic Model Predictive Control that integrates probabilistic constraints and is applicable to probabilistic events with independent and identical distributions. The proposed method employs a technique to approximate the probability of disturbances occurring within the prediction horizon based on historical data. The effectiveness of this model is demonstrated through numerical evaluations of various distribution types, including exponential, uniform, and Poisson distributions.

We suggest new methods for implementing compressive Independent Component Analysis (ICA) on large-scale data sets. These proposed algorithms leverage recent advances in compressive ICA and enhance them for efficient processing of massive data sets by utilizing the stochastic gradient descent optimization technique. The benefits of the new methods are demonstrated through experiments on AIFlow, which enables training of ICA models directly from data distributed across multiple nodes in a distributed system without the need to consolidate it into a single central node. This feature sets our approach apart from the existing compressive ICA solutions and makes it uniquely adaptable to the AIFlow platform.

In an $n$-dimensional lattice where two types of particles interact, a model called the asymmetric noisy voter model randomly selects an adjacent dimension and copies its type, unless a random event occurs with probability $\pi$ and the particle keeps its type. Through computer simulations, it's found that in scenarios with more than one dimension, competition between two types of particles results in either coexistence or extinction, depending on the balance between the dimensions. Additionally, in scenarios with only one dimension, the model shows that the average time until the last particle of one type remains is sub-significant compared to the combinatorial model's average time.

We demonstrate that, under certain assumptions, certain subsets of infinite-dimensional C*-algebras, $M$, infinite-projective in nature, with associated collections of unique ground states, $M_j$, exhibiting finite projectivity levels and satisfying specific 'unique ground state' properties, can transform into type $II_1$ von Neumann algebras in their weak closure when $M_j$ is considered. This finding has the implication that $M$'s weak closure becomes a type $II_1$ factor in scenarios such as condensed matter physics' unique ground state ground states, quantum field theory's Hamiltonian construction, and non-equilibrium quantum states.

A system consisting of two cavities and a coherent loop explores quantum entanglement's boundary under thermal conditions. The influence of thermal noise and loop parameters on generated entanglement is examined. It is found that under specific settings, the entanglement within the qubits remains unaffected by thermal effects, while the light field exhibits increased resilience to thermal effects when the loop is present compared to its absence. The concept of quantum state disentanglement due to thermal effects is defined and used to establish a formula for calculating this limit. The proposed model may have practical applications in the implementation of quantum networks.

A crucial component in calculating precise cross-sections at the one-loop level for massless quarks and gluons is the set of splitting operators that describe the behavior of particles when they become collinear. The present study refines an existing framework by accurately calculating a specific operator associated with the interaction of three collinear particles, specifically the operator related to a triple-glue collinear configuration. The outcome of this calculation has been incorporated into a subtraction method designed to facilitate the calculation of additive physical cross-sections at the one-loop level. The corresponding code for this subtraction method has been integrated into the open-source toolbox known as OpenRapid.

One-dimensional local rings can be significantly simplified using an updated version of Greenberg's strong approximation theorem, specifically when applying it to complete rings with imposed conditions. This updated version of the theorem leads to a new formulation of Hensel's Lemma for rings containing square roots of uniformizers.

This study utilizes the Open Science paradigm, specifically citizen science, to leverage ordinary individuals as science researchers.  By integrating unsupervised learning, the project aims to enhance the efficiency of data processing.  The proposed approach seeks to increase society's awareness of scientific discoveries and historical documentation, with a focus on increasing the number of known sundials in Indonesia through online registration.  By employing machine learning techniques, the project will facilitate the classification of sundial types and facilitate the mapping of related data.

This study introduces the Data and Device-to-Device schemes (DED2D), a novel framework that integrates a data collection layer and a transparent communication layer. We introduce the Time-Forward Information Enhancement Technique (TFIET), a scheme within the DED2D framework, to extend data and energy transmission to users. By leveraging the TFIET, our objective is to minimize the overall transmission time for all users while still meeting their data requirements. Due to the discrete nature of the problem, we convert it into an equivalent optimization issue involving energy allocation and user association, which we then reformulate as a mixed-integer problem. To achieve this, we develop an efficient solution that combines Continuous Value Optimization (CVO) for the energy allocation subproblem and an optimized association method for the user association subproblem. An iterative approach is then employed to find the optimal energy allocation and user association values, ultimately determining the transmission times for all users.

The growing need for remote access and increased demands on laboratories have led to a rise in automated experimental arrangements. A new method for creating automated lab environments is proposed, utilizing virtual-reality technology. This paper outlines this approach, highlighting its benefits and challenges, and compares it to current methods of remote access.

We establish a strong connection between P vs NP and the existence of undirected bipartite graphs with specific properties. Specifically, if Asser's conjecture holds true for bipartite graphs, then there are polynomial-time algorithms for solving NP problems using undirected bipartite graphs, which also validates the Lasso algorithm for bipartite graphs. Conversely, should P not equal NP, we prove that the Lasso problem for bipartite graphs is as difficult as the hardest problems in NP. Additionally, our findings for bipartite graphs open up new questions for further research, including the potential for cross-sections of spectra in general graphs to be in a different complexity class.

We've created a comprehensive theoretical framework for electron probe size/current
distribution, accounting for complex electrostatic phase plate designs. This framework
incorporates detailed pixel patterns and non-ideal plate constructions such as rounded
edges and finite thickness, along with the concept of a 'fill-factor'. Our findings reveal
how these parameters impact electron probe size and current density, particularly for
round probe configurations. Furthermore, we present an analytical solution that relates
the concept of fill-factor to the two-dimensional Fourier transform of a pixel pattern's
auto-correlation function. This solution demonstrates that phase plate current can be
broken down into discrete channels, each carrying distinct electron currents and experiencing
various levels of diffraction. These findings have been validated by simulations and provide
a basis for understanding and measuring phase plate parameters experimentally.

We introduce a comprehensive mathematical structure to describe physical computation processes and their transformation, allowing any mechanism to be considered within a unified framework. This structure, consisting of a category of states and morphisms and a functor representing the computation function, facilitates comparison between different computation methods. A key example is provided for model checking in concurrent systems, demonstrating how various processes can be analyzed and contrasted. We also explore evaluation in abstract terms and propose a model for it. This approach is then applied to quantum computation and a generalization of it known as quantum computation with holes. These processes are shown to fit within the proposed structure and it's argued that they exhibit computational capabilities comparable to classical computation. Furthermore, we propose that there's a connection between the complexity of these processes and its representation within the quantum functor.

We analyze the number of unique locations visited by a simple symmetric random walker in $d$-dimensional space up to a given time frame. When using a random walker in a higher dimension ($d+1$) to count visits on a lower dimension, the counts will significantly overestimate the actual number of visits. In contrast, when using a random walker in a lower dimension ($d-1$) to count visits in a $d$-dimensional space, there's a non-zero probability that the walker will visit every possible point in the space at least once.

In this study, we've developed a model for a polymer black hole based on a mass function, which we then compared to the RESS model for a wormhole. Our analysis revealed that in the non-singular black hole metric, the wormlike nature diminishes as the radial coordinate increases, and at a critical point, it transforms into a Schwarzschild-like solution. Additionally, we found that the energy-momentum tensor for the phantom polymer fluid violates all four energy conditions, and that the behavior of the RESS model and the phantom polymer model are comparable, yet they don't perfectly align.

The influence of quasiparticle velocity reduction on thermodynamic properties in
doped graphene is explored through calculations of temperature-dependent heat
capacity and a model doping function's impact on energy levels in thermodynamic
assessments. Our research demonstrates that quasiparticle velocity reduction by
interactions significantly affects the thermodynamic behavior of doped graphene,
with heat capacity showing distinct properties at low doping levels compared to high
doping levels.

A newly developed system called MaskedSpeech significantly enhances the naturalness and expressiveness of synthesized speech by training speech models on speech encodings MaskedSpeech encodes, which are derived from speech sequences. The system is capable of generating high-quality speech from a single mask, making it highly efficient and resource-friendly. Moreover, MaskedSpeech demonstrates remarkable robustness to various types of test data, including unseen speakers and words, as well as different types of audio masks. Initial results using the FADE encoder show that speech synthesized using MaskedSpeech at a sampling rate of 22050 Hz achieved an unweighted average error rate of 2.37% in a comparison with the original training data at a sampling rate of 16000 Hz. Furthermore, MaskedSpeech achieves comparable performance to full-rank encoders while using significantly fewer parameters, thus making it highly resource-efficient.

High-dimensional regression models often suffer from underperformance due to the inclusion of numerous irrelevant features. Utilizing Bayesian neural networks for such models presents an opportunity, given their efficacy in posterior inference. However, traditional Bayesian analysis becomes impractical with a large number of variables due to the infeasibility of Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling in those cases. To overcome this limitation, we employ a novel approach that leverages Bayesian neural networks through variational inference. This method facilitates efficient learning of complex models and enables the investigation of the relationship between prior and variational posterior distributions. Moreover, our approach ensures the preservation of uncertainty information from the original model, and promotes model interpretability by promoting sparsity. Simulation studies confirm that our technique yields comparable results to state-of-the-art selection techniques while accurately estimating uncertainties and recovering true posterior distributions.

A hybrid of Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attacks and adversarial examples, 
a novel type of attack against Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) emerges, 
where training data is compromised. Notably, this attack differs from 
traditional adversarial example attacks, which target trained DNNs, and can be
further distinguished from past MitM attacks, which exploit knowledge of 
training data without interfering with it. We've developed a DNN attack 
where an attacker has control over a fraction of the training data and can 
manipulate it. The attacker's goal is to cause a shift in the training 
distribution to induce prediction errors in a trained DNN. We've designed 
attacks targeting specific classes or overall network accuracy, and tested 
their effectiveness on three neural networks using the MNIST and CIFAR-10 
datasets. The impact of four parameters on the success of these attacks has 
also been assessed. Notably, our MitM attacks can achieve significant 
prediction errors, surpassing adversarial attacks in some instances, and are 
more challenging to detect due to their subtle effects on model performance.

Recent studies have shown a disproportionate proportion of climate change-related conspiracy theory content on the internet is produced by sources aligned with the US political right. However, these sources are often overlooked by automated systems designed to detect such misinformation. In contrast, prominent platforms promoting climate change skepticism have openly endorsed conspiracy theories, providing unique opportunities for engagement. Focusing on one such platform, David Branch's US Climate Hub, our study analyzes over 10,000 comments from nearly four years of discussions to identify patterns of climate change denial within a predominantly pro-climate community. Our findings reveal the US Climate Hub's role in normalizing conspiracy theories through repeated exposure, despite rare explicit endorsements. Furthermore, our research highlights the community's failure to address these narratives, potentially contributing to the broader dissemination of misinformation.

Researchers at the NA48/2 experiment investigated potential dark matter connections within the double neutral kaon system through an search for proton-electron pairs. The study encompassed two distinct hypotheses: one involving the production of proton-electron pairs via relativistic particles, and another suggesting that the pair is linked to a form of dark matter known as axion-like particles resulting from the decay of a neutral kaon. Both hypotheses were rigorously examined with statistical analysis. Ultimately, significant discoveries were not found, and all results aligned with standard model predictions. In accordance with the axion search standards set by the axion search at the Spallation Neutron Source, observations were found to be consistent but fell short of confirming axion production with a confidence of three standard deviations.

In a non-negotiable exact category, we establish a rigorous framework and investigate intricate relationships surrounding endomorphisms, ext-groups, and duality theorems. Under specific conditions, we identify a criterion for Serre duality and an equivalence between these conditions. Furthermore, we introduce negative duality theorems under certain circumstances, including cases where $\Omega$-rigid objects exist. Regarding exangulated categories, we derive criteria for Serre duality, an object to be $\eta$-rigid, and for n-exangulated categories, we establish criteria for weak n-rigidity. Additionally, we provide examples illustrating distinctiveness of our main results.

Individual education choices are influenced by various factors, including the anticipated earnings from different fields of study.  Although previous studies have examined how students' education decisions relate to their future pay, there is a lack of consensus on the specific mechanisms behind this relationship.  To shed light on this area of research, we have compared post-secondary education choices and their associated earnings in the similar yet distinct environments of Norway and Denmark.  The analysis reveals that fields of study with higher pay potentials attract more students in both nations.  However, we observed signs of excessive specialization among post-secondary students with lower cognitive abilities.  Interestingly, this pattern suggests a greater degree of excessive specialization in Denmark compared to Norway.  The findings also indicate that certain areas of excessive specialization can be attributed to students with lower cognitive abilities seeking fields that offer more direct pathways to employment opportunities.

The 2021 super $J/\psi$ factory has been selected as a key energy region for conducting precision measurements and in-depth analysis at BESIII. This outstanding choice is due to its potential for several novel research opportunities, including: (1) conducting thorough investigations into the rare decays of charmed mesons and mixed $B$-meson mixing; (2) Examining time-dependent mixing in D0 mesons; (3) Investigate the underlying principles of flavor and matter-antimatter imbalance in charm baryons; (4) Investigate the internal structure of charmed nuclei.

To understand how accretion onto a three-star system works, we developed a mathematical model to simulate the behavior of a binary star orbiting a larger mass. Our results show that in a large, hierarchical system, the smaller stars will gain more mass and undergo more significant growth compared to a single star of equivalent mass. The extent of this mass gain depends on factors such as system size, stellar mass, and orbital distance. For a certain range of parameters, our study indicates that a binary star can quickly grow and become a massive object, potentially leading to exotic stellar types and high-mass black holes. The rapid growth of a binary star can also be used as a theoretical explanation for certain black hole mergers that have been observed through their gravitational waves. The potential applications of our model include a more comprehensive understanding of stellar evolution, particularly for massive stars, and the evolution of star clusters.

The distribution of matter in the universe is not uniform, necessitating a departure from the standard Friedmann equations that govern its evolution. Incorporating an initial inhomogeneous distribution, we rederive the matter density's effect on the universe's overall structure, ultimately determining its homogeneous outcome. This revised model not only rectifies a longstanding issue with the dust matter equation but also yields an equation that aligns asymptotically with the well-established Friedmann equation.

This article proposes a novel method for identifying and segmenting defective images in the presence of noise, by combining the piecewise constant Mumford-Shah model with a new, flexible total variation functional tailored for color images. To enhance the efficiency of the approach, the study utilizes the alternating minimization technique, which involves switching between two tasks: rectifying the image in a piecewise manner and updating the identified regions. Furthermore, the algorithm incorporates a constraint to ensure that each segment represents a distinct color, resulting in improved segmentation outcomes for high-quality color images. Experimental findings demonstrate the algorithm's capability to successfully recover and segment defective color images with segmented boundaries that align closely with actual object edges.

Recent observations from the Euclid satellite have detected B-mode polarization patterns in the Milky Way's gravitational wave background. These B-modes are attributed to foreground interference from dust emission. Analysis indicates a significant correlation between these B-modes and dust intensity at lag lengths exceeding 100 microarcseconds. To investigate this phenomenon, researchers simulated the effects of an ultra-light axion-like particle that could constitute dark matter, under the assumption that its distribution creates interference patterns in light. However, when random fluctuations in photon counts are taken into account, simulations fail to replicate the observed lag lengths, implying that such a particle would need to be heavier than 10^-21 eV to explain the data.

A cutting-edge approach to computing, known as neuromorphic computing, capitalizes on VLSI hardware to implement algorithms mimicking the human brain. By emulating synaptic behaviors, this technique enables learning on the chip itself, distinct from traditional online learning methods. To adapt neural networks for neuromorphic systems, we have developed an algorithm for adjusting the weights and biases of layers comprising integrate-and-fire neurons, which mimics brain plasticity mechanisms like Hebbian learning and delta-rule-based learning. We have implemented this algorithm on a 40MHz FPGA and evaluated its efficacy by applying it to a set of 10000 MNIST images.

We employed the Radio Telescope for Coronal Studies in studies of a notable coronal mass ejection event, specifically the storm on June 12th, 2017. Our analysis focused on the coronal structures surrounding three prominent storm sources during this period. We identified and tracked magnetic bright points associated with two storm sources, revealing a correlation between the storms and these points. Our observations indicated a relationship between the storm's intensity and size, showing that the storm's evolution followed a pattern of mode growth. Furthermore, the movement of two bright points suggested a physical connection between them, and the expansion of these points aligned with the plasma outflow during the coronal mass ejection. Our results also indicated the presence of magnetic recombination and reconnection processes that contributed to the coronal mass ejection.

We have developed an integrated mirrorless magneto-optical trap that integrates the vapor cell and optical components on a chip, allowing for a highly compact and cost-effective quantum sensor. By using a chip-integrated approach, all necessary lasers can be coupled into the chip with just a single laser source, where a 709 nm laser provides the necessary transitions for optically trapping atoms and a 354.5 nm harmonic wavelength enables efficient detection through a highly sensitive detector and on-chip integrated readout circuitry. The chip-based MOT achieves a record high detection rate of over 99.99% per microsecond for a population of around 3000 microscopically hot rubidium atoms, and the integration of the chip-based MOT and detector enables high-speed operation of around 100 kHz for quantum sensing applications.

A theoretical model is proposed to address the low luminosity of supermassive black holes such as Sgr A* and M87*. The model suggests that the radio emissions are produced by external astroparticles, specifically high-energy particles generated by cosmic ray protons interacting with electrons in the vicinity of the black hole, forming a plasma that releases the required energy. This interaction leads to the dissipation of energy and the creation of the observed jet, with the particle plasmoid located at the base of the jet experiencing intense pressure and being confined by magnetic fields. The plasmoid's composition includes hot plasma and magnetic fields, with the plasmoid being ejected as the jet and emitting synchrotron radiation. The model is consistent with the observed luminosity of black holes, with the interaction between the plasmoid and the jet explaining the observed luminosity and spectrum of M87* and other black holes. The model also has implications for the observed luminosity and spectrum of other black holes, with the plasmoid being ejected as the jet and emitting synchrotron radiation.

We investigate the impact of neutral atom motion parallel to a reflective surface on photon emission and energy dissipation. This effect is quantified through the rate of photon emission and the radiation pressure it exerts on the atom. Additionally, the radiation spectrum of the atom-mirror system is analyzed, and conditions for the emergence of distinct spectral features are established.

The purpose of this note is to establish a link between the application of the minimax principle and the presence of a geometric structure on the function being optimized. The minimax principle is used to guarantee the existence of a solution to a problem, while the function's geometry is defined by its critical sets and the associated category.

This research presents an innovative approach that integrates a handwritten text recognizer with a generative model, specifically designed to enhance the quality of severely damaged images. We achieve this by combining existing low-light image enhancement techniques with a new module that incorporates feedback from the handwritten text recognizer. This feedback-driven module is implemented as two interconnected neural networks, which simulate a signal processing pipeline. By utilizing this approach, we successfully restore the characteristics of modern printing processes in degraded documents. Consequently, our method enhances the performance of the handwritten text recognizer on extremely deteriorated images, thereby allowing for the accurate recognition of intricate textual content in historically significant documents.

Text mining from textless IDs poses a complex challenge, particularly since id cards idiosyncratically vary, making it difficult to process. Existing approaches have limitations, particularly in their inability to account for the potential presence or absence of information on id cards, leading to incorrect conclusions when information is missing. In contrast, we propose a novel deep learning-based model that accurately extracts information from id cards, specifically targeting Chinese IDs. This model incorporates a unique attention mechanism that prioritizes key features, and a multi-task learning framework that simultaneously extracts information and identifies card types. Furthermore, we introduce an algorithm to optimize the extraction process by considering potential information gaps. Our model not only excels in extraction accuracy, achieving an 89.6% recognition rate for key digits, but also efficiently identifies card types with a 98.8% accuracy across various categories.

In complex scenarios such as dense urban areas, channel estimation is challenging due to a large number of channel parameters that need to be estimated. Traditional methods often discard prior knowledge, relying instead on pilot signals, to estimate these parameters. However, a pilot-based approach alone may not be sufficient for accurately characterizing channels in highly mobile situations. This research introduces a long short term memory network that leverages learned information from previous channels to enhance estimation performance. By incorporating an LSTM layer after initial estimation, the network refines its predictions and minimizes errors. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed estimation method outperforms traditional techniques by significantly reducing errors, especially in high mobility situations.

Our strategy incorporates an established astronomical image super-resolution technique and builds upon it by integrating an image enhancement component. The original approach utilizes low-resolution images to generate higher-resolution versions. By adding the image enhancement aspect, we refine the quality of astronomical images at higher resolutions. Specifically, our dual tasks are executed within an unsupervised framework, using only paired datasets consisting of blurred and sharp images as training samples. Our method stands out from existing approaches by not requiring a high-resolution training dataset, instead, it uses the information from astronomical images to directly produce enhanced images at higher resolutions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by training and testing models on datasets from various sources, including the Gaia survey, simulated images, and external datasets.

A novel optimization framework is presented for producing lightweight neural networks with predetermined architectures by training a governing equation-based network. The underlying principles of this framework stem from the distributed nature and capacity for parameter sharing inherent in neural networks. In particular, it offers a means to produce models resistant to overfitting, even with limited datasets, and yields well-organized, sparse models through its built-in sparsity-inducing approach. The efficacy of this framework is validated through experiments in 3D  point cloud registration and estimation of 3D object poses, where it consistently generates efficient models requiring fewer parameters and computations than state-of-the-art alternatives, while matching their accuracy.

In 2019, the European Committee for Future Accelerators (ECFA) set up a task force to support young researchers, which started operations in April 2020. This group is composed of professionals with relevant experience in education, mentorship, and young professionals' development within the particle accelerator and detector fields. After a needs assessment and strategic planning in the summer of 2020, the task force developed a comprehensive educational program for its first event in November 2020. The ECFA established the 'Early Career Researcher' (ECR) panel to continue its efforts and organize a series of workshops focusing on high-energy physics career paths. The panel held its first meeting in November 2020 and will hold subsequent workshops throughout 2021. Additionally, the panel will oversee the development of educational materials and will guide ECR activities for the next few years.

We have developed a simple and effective method to control line waves in the visible light spectrum using an ultrathin patch of graphene. The graphone metasurface, consisting of a graphene layer and a dielectric patch, enables the creation of static potentials that control the movement of light. Our research demonstrates how this technology can be used to create and control straight and curved line states, as well as how it can be applied to break time symmetry and control the flow of light. Additionally, we have shown how the graphone patch can be used to create static gravitational fields that control the movement of light similar to $\rm{M^3}$ materials.

This study presents a method to model multi-human multi-robot interactions (HMRIs) using a framework that leverages Federated Learning (FL). To address the issue of private movement data, the framework combines a FL-based machine learning approach with a social model. The FL algorithm trains a global model through the sharing of gradients, not data, while the social model explains the observed behavior, creating transparency. As a result, the framework enables the sharing of private data without compromising confidentiality and provides a means to understand the system's behavior. A series of simulation experiments demonstrate the system's capabilities in multiple scenarios.

A novel method for bias-reduced estimation of population quantiles has been developed. This method leverages nonparametric density estimation techniques and does not require a specified distribution assumption. Unlike previous approaches, the proposed method improves upon the standard rate of convergence from $n^{-1/2}$ to $n^{-1}$, and addresses issues related to bias reduction that often result in non-smooth estimates. By employing a bandwidth optimization approach, bias is further minimized without sacrificing consistency. This method has been successfully applied to sample distribution monitoring, demonstrating its effectiveness.

A new task in link prediction involves identifying which nodes in a knowledge graph are connected. This is achieved by translating external information, used in previous research for extracting relationships and categories, into a predictive model. The method's performance in a standard benchmark is enhanced by combining multiple transformed versions of the input data through an ensemble approach. The results indicate that this technique significantly outperforms existing link prediction methods with an impressive reduction in errors.

In the context of a strongly coupled N=4 super Yang-Mills theory, researchers have derived the Debye mass, considering both adjoint and fundamental representations, while disregarding the effects of velocity. A key finding is that the Debye mass types differ when a baryonic chemical potential is introduced. Through the application of the large N limit, it was determined that the Debye mass in the fundamental representation scales as 1/N, while the Debye mass from the adjoint representation can be expressed as a combination of the potential's influence and a contribution that arises from fundamental representation, which they refer to as the "pyramid rule." This relationship was utilized to infer properties of Debye masses in a QCD context, particularly in situations involving only fundamental representation, such as heavy-ion collisions.

A study on the magnetic properties of Tb3RuO7 and Nd3RuO7 was conducted using neutron diffraction to examine the magnetic structures of these compounds. Both compounds exhibit a hexagonal crystal structure with space group P6_3/mmc. In both Tb3RuO7 and Nd3RuO7, the rare earth ions (Tb or Nd) are found to have a ferromagnetic arrangement along the c-axis below their respective transition temperatures of 1.1 K and 2.2 K. However, the ruthenium ions (Ru1 and Ru2) display different behavior, exhibiting ferromagnetic ordering aligned with the c-axis for Tb3RuO7 but showing in-plane antiferromagnetic ordering for Nd3RuO7. Notably, there is a significant induced magnetic moment observed on the Ru ions in both compounds.

A key aspect of deep learning's success lies in its ability to adapt to a diverse range of real-world problems. The complexity of models and their design have traditionally been closely tied to their architecture, with improvements often requiring in-depth expertise in model design. The introduction of generic building blocks and frameworks has somewhat reduced this dependency, but models specific to the underlying method are still required, involving time-consuming trial and error processes. The situation is further complicated by models being tightly linked to their optimization methods, necessitating adjustments in the underlying algorithm for improvements. The Local-Functional Representation provides a framework where the underlying method's flexibility allows for seamless adaptation to various applications without modifying the technique itself. The LFR combines simple components and their interactions to form a cohesive model, resulting in improved understanding and adaptation. The Local-Functional Representation exhibits several beneficial characteristics, such as requiring less data, being more interpretable, and being capable of generalizing to a diverse range of signals beyond the training set. We demonstrate these properties through a series of experiments and provide a theoretical analysis of the RFR's properties, along with a discussion on its applications in reinforcement learning and the prediction of interacting particles.

We introduce a novel semi-generative model that captures the intricate connections between the objectives a system seeks to achieve and the data it processes. This model posits a set of latent variables representing the influence of underlying causes on the target, separate variables representing potential effects, and a distinct set of variables representing possible outcomes. A unique aspect of our model is that it permits effects to originate from sources other than the target variable itself. To effectively uncover these interdependencies, we employ variational inference techniques. This approach has been successfully applied to a range of complex domains, including predicting a company's performance based on its financial reports, determining an individual's health status based on medical records, and analyzing voting patterns based on survey responses. Our results demonstrate that our proposed semi-generative model consistently outperforms traditional causal discovery methods in uncovering hidden relationships within observational data.

The presence of an underlying geometric framework in deep learning systems is evident, and by employing this concept, researchers in geometry and deep learning collaborate to jointly develop new algorithms, geometric structures, and models. This concept is further reinforced by an analytical and computational geometry that applies to this domain.

We examine three groups of cubic fields, defined by their minimal extension from Q using a specific cubic equation. By selecting different quadratic components for this equation, we can influence the characteristics of the cubic field. Our research compares and contrasts these influences.

We examine LRP, a popular approach for interpreting deep neural networks, providing an overview of its principles, historical context, and theoretical aspects. Recent LRP developments are discussed, including various propagation strategies, and their applications in enhancing model performance and visualizing model behavior and features.

A parameter `r` introduces a new family of Stirling numbers of the second kind, defined as `r-associated Stirling numbers, which only become positive when `r` is less than or equal to the product of `n` and `k`. This positivity constraint hinders the development of significant theoretical properties for this family. To overcome this limitation, we propose a negative generalization, allowing the positivity constraint to be bypassed, and further extend this to Stirling cycles and derive a new family of generalized Bernoulli numbers, exhibiting favorable properties.

The concept of irreducible domains has gained significant attention in condense matter physics, particularly in the study of materials with layered structures. The concept is used to categorize different physical phenomena based on the type of symmetry breaking that occurs. We present a mathematical framework for identifying irreducible domains in layered materials, which allows us to classify various irreducible domains based on polarizations and orbitals in dipolar and quadrupolar materials, as well as predict new phenomena in bisphenol gas and nickel oxide.

A method is proposed for calculating upper limits on the attainable momentum
momenta in experiments of arbitrary nature and settings. These limits are imposed
by physical processes on their respective systems. The concept of higher
momenta is comparable to light with wavelengths smaller than the given system's
dimensions, which is analogous to using smaller cells for modeling a smooth
manifold.

We present a innovative technique to accelerate Monte Carlo simulations by utilizing complex-valued affine coupling layers. This method builds upon recent advancements in complex neural networks and probabilistic modeling by integrating the efficiency of complex numbers with the power of learned transformations on complex-valued distributions. The simulation process involves sequentially applying multiple coupled normal distributions with complex parameters, where the means and variances are determined by a function applied to the preceding state. The efficiency of this approach stems from the ability to perform affine operations on complex numbers, thereby reducing computational costs and memory usage. The method also demonstrates substantial speedup in Monte Carlo simulations and is compatible with existing models such as complex VAEs and SAE, while we provide evidence of its effectiveness through empirical evaluations.

We investigate a model featuring a broken U(1)_F flavor symmetry in a gauge group of SU(5), utilizing discrete R-parity for stabilization. By introducing discrete Z2F symmetry, we analyze how this stabilizes the residual flavor symmetry after U(1)_F breaking. In the late stages of breaking, the residual Z2F symmetry ensures the cancellation of flavor anomalies, leading to controlled quasi-spontaneous breaking of U(1)_F and an explanation for the significant top-bottom quark mass disparity. Furthermore, in a non-supersymmetric framework, the stabilizing Z2F symmetry can yield real and positive masses for the Higgs bosons within a milder version of the Standard Model.

Virtual machine management solutions typically rely on applets to manage and
control virtual machines, providing an interface for various operational functions.
Although this setup offers convenience, it also presents an opportunity for
adversaries to exploit vulnerable intermediate representations, such as those
used in Virtual Machine Command (VMC) and Virtual Machine Property (VPPM), for
both information exposure and system manipulation purposes. This study examines
the vulnerabilities associated with VMC and VPPM in these formats, conducting a
comprehensive analysis involving over 1000 applets. As a result, we identified
13 exploitation techniques and created corresponding tools in our open-source
project called VirtSec. To mitigate these threats, we developed 13 defensive
methods, which when implemented in a security layer, show a 99.9% reduction in
exploitable cases. Additionally, we designed a framework for an automated security
inspection process, allowing users to identify potential vulnerabilities in user-
supplied data, thereby enhancing system resilience and reliability.

The effectiveness of pre-trained language models in zero-shot tasks has led researchers to explore whether these models can be transferred to unseen languages. This study investigates the theoretical underpinnings of this issue by examining how different characteristics affect a model's ability to adapt to new languages. Consequently, a new evaluation framework is developed, and relevant metrics are identified. These metrics are applied to compare various multilingual pre-trained models, providing insights into whether these models are trained in a way that accommodates a wide range of languages. Ultimately, this research guides further training efforts to enhance the cross-lingual applicability of these models.

The results show that as the angular velocity increases, the binary mass decreases and the most massive binary formed a single star. We introduce a novel kernel-based reduction technique that significantly speeds up the m-arctan kernel function's computational complexity while maintaining its advantages. This method speeds up m-arK by at least a factor of $O(k)$ compared to traditional linear kernels of the same complexity. Our method also retains kernel properties and flexibility, and we enhance it with an unsupervised filter to eliminate outliers. Furthermore, we propose multiple strategies to choose the optimal projected dimensionality. Experimental results demonstrate that m-ar-K based projections exceed the performance of other high-dimensional data visualization techniques.

This research explores the implications of a hypothetical class called EPC on computational complexity. We propose that a substantial advancement in understanding the relationship between CPT and PTIME could result from a super-polynomial lower bound being established for EPC. Conversely, a significant proof linking CPT to PTIME could arise from a suprapolynomial upper bound for EPC. We also find that EPC is connected to a class known as QFPE when a particular condition, $NP^C \subseteq PH^C$, is met under the assumption of an oracle C. Furthermore, we show that EPC contains a problem called MIN-2-CSP-3 under the assumption of unique games being efficiently solvable, and MIN-2-CSP-3 may be equal to C-PTIME under specific conditions.

A ring R is defined as $\tau$-elementary if it satisfies a specific condition, and its $\tau$-elementary quotient ring is then described. The definitions and properties of these terms allow for a comprehensive understanding of certain ring theory theorems. In this context, a series of established theorems are presented: (R1-R9), which were contributed by multiple researchers. Specifically, (R1) and (R2) were established by Guralnick and Leptin, and further work was done by researchers including Guralnick, and those cited in [10] and [11]. In addition, (R3) and others were contributed by various other researchers, and these theorems address various ring theory properties.

their widespread usage. Recognizing social media platforms' growing role in
deliberation, it is essential to gain an understanding of online conversations.
Consequently, multiple projects have been established to analyze public debates on social media.
